Empirical Research Plan – “The Long-Run Effect of Colonialism on Income in Island Nations”

=====================================================================
1. Identification Strategy
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Two–Stage Least Squares (Instrumental-Variables) in a cross-section of islands, augmented with archipelago (or regional) fixed effects.

Why IV?  
• The “treatment” (ever being a colony, or type/length of colonial rule) occurred centuries ago; we have no reliable pre-treatment income series, so DID/event-study is infeasible.  
• Colonial status is likely endogenous to unobserved determinants of long-run income (e.g., natural resources, strategic location).  
• Geography generated quasi-random exposure to European powers because sailing-ship technology made some islands easier to reach than others. This gives us plausibly exogenous instruments.

Proposed instruments (Z):  
1. Sailing-distance from Lisbon/Seville/London in the 16th century following prevailing winds (“Great-Circle with Wind” route length).  
2. Whether the island lies within the historical doldrums belt (0–10° latitude) that impeded early European ships.  
3. Natural deep-harbor availability (binary from modern nautical charts).  

These variables strongly predict colonial take-over probabilities but are unlikely to affect 21st-century GDP per capita except through colonial history.

=====================================================================
2. Treatment and Control
---------------------------------------------------------------------
• Treatment variable D: Indicator = 1 if island i was ever formally colonised by a European power between 1400-1960 (alternative specifications: years under colonial rule; coloniser identity dummies).  
• Control group: Islands that were never colonies (e.g., Tonga, Japan’s smaller islands pre-Meiji, Iceland), plus those settled only by indigenous peoples.  
• Timing: Not needed for cross-section IV; we treat colonial exposure as a historical stock.  
• No running variable/cutoff (not RDD).

=====================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
---------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Instrument relevance – Geography variables must predict colonial status.  
Plausible: Sailing distance and harbor quality were first-order determinants of European expansion.

A2. Exclusion restriction – The instruments affect contemporary GDP only through colonial exposure, not through alternative channels.  
Plausibility: Modern shipping technology eliminates 16th-century sailing constraints; deep harbors matter today, but we control for current port capacity and natural resource endowments.

A3. Independence – Conditional on controls and archipelago fixed effects, the instruments are as-good-as-random with respect to unobserved determinants of long-run income.  
Plausible but needs careful control set (island size, fertility of soil, distance to markets today, etc.).

A4. Monotonicity – Islands closer/easier to reach were (weakly) more likely to be colonised for every realisation of unobservables.  
Reasonable: No evidence of “defiers” (islands that were easier to reach but systematically not colonised).

A5. SUTVA – One island’s colonial status does not affect another’s GDP directly (beyond global equilibrium effects).  
Fair for small islands; we cluster by archipelago to be conservative.

=====================================================================
4. Main Threats & Mitigations
---------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Instrument violates exclusion because geographic ease of access still matters for trade today.  
Mitigation: Include modern shipping-cost control (distance to major container route), airline-distance to global markets, natural deep-harbor indicator interacted with post-1970 containerisation dummy. Run robustness dropping trade-dependent micro-states (Singapore, Bahamas).

T2. Omitted pre-colonial development—some islands attractive to Europeans were already richer.  
Mitigation: Control for archaeological proxies of pre-contact population density; restrict sample to islands with no written-language societies pre-1500; include archipelago fixed effects.

T3. Measurement error in colonial duration/type.  
Mitigation: Use multiple historical sources; run alternative treatment definitions (binary ever-colonised; years under rule; coloniser identity). Classical measurement error in treatment is corrected by IV.

=====================================================================
5. R Code Outline
---------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data
library(fixest)       # IV + fixed effects
library(lmtest)       # tests
library(sandwich)
library(tidyverse)

# 1. Load Data -------------------------------------------------------
islands <- fread("island_colonial_dataset.csv")  # one row per island

# 2. Variable Construction ------------------------------------------
islands[, treated      := as.integer(ever_colony == 1)]
islands[, ln_gdppc_2020 := log(gdp_pc_2020)]

# Instruments
islands[, wind_dist_km    := sailing_distance_km]  # 16th-century route length
islands[, doldrums        := as.integer(abs(latitude) < 10)]
islands[, deep_harbor     := as.integer(natural_harbor == "Yes")]

# Controls
islands[, ln_area         := log(area_sqkm)]
islands[, ln_pop1500      := log(pop_1500 + 1)]
islands[, ln_dist_world   := log(distance_to_major_market_km)]

# 3. Main IV Regression ---------------------------------------------
iv_main <- feols(
  ln_gdppc_2020 ~ 1 | treated ~ wind_dist_km + doldrums + deep_harbor | archipelago_id,
  data = islands, vcov = ~archipelago_id
)
summary(iv_main, stage = 1)  # shows first-stage F

# 4. Robustness: Alternative Treatment = Years of Colonial Rule -----
islands[, years_colony := end_year - start_year]
iv_years <- feols(
  ln_gdppc_2020 ~ 1 | years_colony ~ wind_dist_km + doldrums + deep_harbor | archipelago_id,
  data = islands, vcov = ~archipelago_id
)
summary(iv_years, stage = 1)

# 5. Over-identification (Hansen J) ---------------------------------
library(AER)
iv_aer <- ivreg(
  ln_gdppc_2020 ~ treated + ln_area + ln_pop1500 | 
  wind_dist_km + doldrums + deep_harbor + ln_area + ln_pop1500,
  data = islands
)
summary(iv_aer, diagnostics = TRUE)

# 6. Save Results ----------------------------------------------------
saveRDS(list(main = iv_main, years = iv_years, aer = iv_aer), "iv_results.rds")
```

=====================================================================
6. Expected Results
---------------------------------------------------------------------
Prior: Being colonised should lower current GDP per capita for most islands because colonial institutions favored extraction, created ethnic stratification, and discouraged diversified growth. Expect a negative effect of roughly −0.5 log-points (≈ 40 % lower income) relative to never-colonised islands, but with heterogeneity (British colonies may fare better than Spanish/French).

=====================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV method)
---------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument relevance (first-stage F > 10) .............. 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction believable ........................ 0.5  
C3: Independence from unobservables after controls .......... 0.5  
C4: Monotonicity (no “defiers”) ............................. 1  
C5: SUTVA / no interference ................................. 1  
TOTAL (out of 5): 4.0

=====================================================================
The plan exploits exogenous geographic variation in colonial exposure to estimate its long-run causal effect on island incomes, while transparently laying out assumptions, threats, and robustness steps.
